claims.text: Replacing 20% of the Hf sublattice with Sc forms Hf0.8Sc0.2MoTaTiZr, corresponding to approximately Hf16Sc4Mo20Ta20Ti20Zr20 at%.
Substituting Sc for Hf will reduce the alloy density because Sc has a lower atomic mass than Hf.
The Sc substitution will reduce density by at least 5%, from 10.21 to approximately 9.7 g cm−3.
Sc substitution will refine the alloy's grains.
Sc substitution will increase lattice distortion because of atomic-size and electrochemical differences between Sc and the other alloying elements.
The increased lattice distortion will produce solid-solution strengthening.
Grain refinement will increase grain-boundary area.
Solid-solution strengthening and grain refinement will maintain the modified alloy's strength and ductility.
The modified alloy will have a room-temperature yield strength of at least 1500 MPa.
The modified alloy will have a yield strength of at least 800 MPa at 1000 °C.
The modified alloy will have a fracture toughness of at least 20 MPa m^(1/2).
As-cast HfMoTaTiZr has a density of 10.21 g cm−3.
As-cast HfMoTaTiZr has a room-temperature yield strength of 1600 MPa.
As-cast HfMoTaTiZr has an elevated-temperature yield strength of 855 MPa.

contradictions.description: The stated boundary covers room temperature through 1600 °C, but the controlled experiment measures mechanical properties only at room temperature and 1000 °C, so it cannot test performance across the full claimed range.

The hypothesis says performance will be maintained without sacrifice, while the predicted thresholds permit yield-strength reductions from 1600 to 1500 MPa and from 855 to 800 MPa, and the rejection rule permits reductions of up to 10%.
